title: The Medieval Northwest
subtitle: 632–1517 · A Corridor of the Hajj Roads — the Oases, the Tribes, and the Cities of Thamūd

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: A region with no state of its own — the conquered oases under the caliphs, the tribes holding the wells, the small emirate at Dūmah, and the Egyptian and Syrian overlords who ran the two Hajj roads that crossed it

entries.label: The northwest under the caliphs
entries.loc: Wādī al-Qurā and the oases, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The conquered oases were held by governors from Medina and then Damascus; the Jews of Khaybar and Fadak were expelled under ʿUmar; and the region was demoted from a frontier to a pilgrim corridor between Syria and the holy cities.
entries.note: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-buldān; the early Islamic administration of the Hejaz.

entries.label: Wādī al-Qurā and the early Islamic oases
entries.loc: Wādī al-Qurā, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: 'The valley of the villages' and the string of oases along the route were a real agricultural district in the first Islamic centuries — taxed, settled and productive — before a long decline set in.
entries.note: Yāqūt, Muʿjam al-buldān, on Wādī al-Qurā; al-Muqaddasī.

entries.group: The Bedouin Northwest and the Hajj Emirates (969–1517)
entries.label: The bedouin northwest
entries.loc: the northwestern steppe and oases
entries.hint: As the caliphate weakened the region belonged to its tribes — the Balī, the Juhayna, the Banū ʿAṭiyya, and from the north the Shammar and the ʿAnaza — who held the wells and either taxed or raided the pilgrim caravans.
entries.note: the tribal geographies in the medieval and later sources; Max von Oppenheim, 'Die Beduinen'.

entries.group: The Bedouin Northwest and the Hajj Emirates (969–1517)
entries.label: Dūmat al-Jandal and the small emirates
entries.loc: Dūmat al-Jandal, al-Jawf, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The oasis of al-Jawf, held by the Kalb and then by others, was a minor emirate with its own fort — the Marid castle — at the far northern edge of the pilgrim world, where the routes to Syria and Iraq forked.
entries.note: Yāqūt on Dūmat al-Jandal; the Italian–Saudi excavations of the Marid castle and the oasis.

entries.group: The Hajj Roads and their Overlords (632–1517)
entries.label: The overlords of the Hajj roads
entries.loc: Damascus and Cairo · running the routes through the northwest
entries.hint: The caliphs, then the Fatimids and the sharifs, then above all the Mamluks of Egypt ran the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrim roads through the northwest — garrisoning the stations, digging the wells, and paying the tribes to let the caravans pass.
entries.note: Suraiya Faroqhi and the earlier literature on the Hajj roads; Andrew Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route'.

entries.label: Qurḥ, Taymāʾ and Khaybar
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA (Qurḥ), Taymāʾ and Khaybar, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Qurḥ (al-Mābiyāt) near old Dadān was a market town and a mint on the Hajj road through the 13th century; Taymāʾ held on under local families; and Khaybar, notoriously malarial, shrank to a fever-ridden group of villages.
entries.note: the al-Mābiyāt / Qurḥ excavations; the medieval geographers on the oasis towns.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The expulsion that ended the Jewish oases, the chronic raiding of the pilgrim caravans, and the tribal migrations that redrew the human map

entries.label: The expulsion of the Jews
entries.loc: Khaybar and Fadak, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: ʿUmar removed the Jewish communities of Khaybar and Fadak to Syria and Iraq, on the tradition that the Prophet had said two religions could not remain in the Hejaz — the end of the ancient Jewish oases, and of the region's oldest continuous settlement.
entries.note: al-Balādhurī; the debated historicity of the ʿUmar expulsion; Michael Lecker on the Khaybar Jews.

entries.label: The tribes and the pilgrim caravans
entries.loc: the Syrian and Egyptian Hajj routes
entries.hint: The raiding of the Hajj caravans by the tribes of the route, the surra payments that bought passage, and the periodic massacres when a subsidy lapsed or a caravan lost its way — the chronic low war of the corridor for nine centuries.
entries.note: the Hajj-disaster notices in the chronicles; Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994) for the later pattern.

entries.label: The wars of the bedouin northwest
entries.loc: the northwestern steppe
entries.hint: The southward push of the Shammar and the ʿAnaza from the 15th century, and the feuds over the wells and the grazing that came with it, reshaped the tribal map of the region on the eve of the Ottoman period.
entries.note: the tribal migration literature; the northern Arabian tribal geographies.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The disputed oasis estate of Fadak, the administration of the Hajj roads, and the subsidy that bought the corridor's safety

entries.label: The Fadak affair
entries.loc: Fadak (al-Ḥāʾiṭ), Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The oasis of Fadak, a personal estate of the Prophet, became a contested property — claimed by Fāṭima, held by the state, granted to the ʿAlids by sympathetic caliphs and taken back by others. A small oasis carried a large weight of Sunni–Shiʿi dispute.
entries.note: al-Balādhurī and the Shiʿi sources on Fadak; the fullest treatment in Wilferd Madelung, 'The Succession to Muḥammad' (1997).

entries.label: The administration of the Hajj roads
entries.loc: Damascus and Cairo · to Medina
entries.hint: The amīr al-ḥajj of Damascus and of Cairo, the fixed stages, the wells and the small forts, and the surra to the tribes — the logistical machine that ran the pilgrimage reached down through the northwest and was most of what governed it.
entries.note: Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Hajj-road literature.

entries.label: The surra and the tribal subsidy
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes
entries.hint: The annual payment in money and grain from Damascus and Cairo to the tribes of the route was a transfer of wealth into a poor region in exchange for the caravans' safety — and the single largest economic fact of the medieval northwest.
entries.note: the surra registers (later, Ottoman, with medieval roots); Faroqhi (1994).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Nabataean tombs read as the ruined cities of Thamūd, the pilgrim road as a sacred landscape, and the fading of the last Jewish communities

entries.label: Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ and the Thamūd
entries.loc: Hegra (Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ), Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Medieval Muslims identified the Nabataean tombs of Hegra with the Qurʾanic people of Thamūd, destroyed for rejecting the prophet Ṣāliḥ. The site became a place of dread that pilgrims were told to hurry past without stopping or drinking its water.
entries.note: the Qurʾan 7:73–79, 11:61–68; the ḥadīth of the Prophet hurrying his men past al-Ḥijr at Tabūk; Ibn Jubayr, Riḥla.

entries.label: The pilgrim road as a religious landscape
entries.loc: Tabūk, al-ʿUlA and the route, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The shrine of the prophet Ṣāliḥ, the mosque where the Prophet was said to have prayed at Tabūk, the local saints and the Sufi lodges of the route — a sacred geography laid over the corridor by the twice-yearly traffic of the Hajj.
entries.note: the Hajj-guide literature (the dalīl al-Hajj); the shrine notices in the geographers.

entries.label: The last Jews and the end of a presence
entries.loc: Taymāʾ and Wādī al-Qurā, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Small Jewish communities lingered at Taymāʾ and Wādī al-Qurā for some centuries after ʿUmar's expulsion, and a legend of a surviving Jewish tribe at Khaybar persisted into modern times — but the ancient Jewish northwest was effectively gone by the high medieval period.
entries.note: the traveller reports chasing the Khaybar legend; Newby, 'A History of the Jews of Arabia' (1988).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The mudbrick old town of al-ʿUlA, the early Islamic rock inscriptions of the routes, the Hajj-road wells and forts, and the excavated market town of Qurḥ

entries.label: The old town of al-ʿUlA
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The dense labyrinth of mudbrick houses — sharing walls, roofed lanes, a single defensible mass — that grew up from the 13th century as Qurḥ declined. A classic Hejazi oasis town, inhabited until the 1980s and now conserved.
entries.note: the al-ʿUlA old town conservation project (Royal Commission for AlUla); the earlier surveys by the Saudi antiquities department.

entries.label: The early Islamic rock inscriptions
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The enormous corpus of dated and undated Arabic graffiti along the routes — including some of the earliest dated Islamic inscriptions anywhere, such as the Zuhayr inscription of 24 AH (644–45) near al-ʿUlA, written a decade after the Prophet's death.
entries.note: the Zuhayr inscription; the Saudi and international epigraphic surveys of the northwestern routes (Frédéric Imbert and others).

entries.label: The Hajj-road wells and forts
entries.loc: the Syrian and Egyptian routes, northwest Arabia
entries.hint: The reservoirs, cisterns and small forts built and rebuilt along the two pilgrim roads by the caliphs, the Fatimids and the Mamluks — the medieval water and security infrastructure that the Ottomans inherited and expanded after 1517.
entries.note: Petersen (2012); the archaeology of the pre-Ottoman Hajj stations.

entries.label: Qurḥ, the vanished market town
entries.loc: al-Mābiyāt (Qurḥ), near al-ʿUlA, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The excavated remains of al-Mābiyāt — its houses, its congregational mosque, its pottery kilns and its coins — give the fullest picture of a medieval Hejazi town on the pilgrim road, abandoned by the 14th century and never rebuilt.
entries.note: the al-Mābiyāt excavations (King Saud University; later the RCU); the Qurḥ coinage.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The geographers' detailed itineraries of the corridor, the travellers on the road, and the early-Islamic epigraphy that is the region's richest medieval record

entries.label: The geographers on the northwest
entries.loc: the northwestern corridor
entries.hint: Al-Muqaddasī, al-Iṣṭakhrī, Yāqūt's Muʿjam al-buldān and the Hajj-road itineraries described the oases, the wells, the tribes and the distances of the corridor — a well-documented route through an otherwise thinly-documented land.
entries.note: al-Muqaddasī, Aḥsan al-taqāsīm; Yāqūt, Muʿjam al-buldān; Ibn Rusta and the road-books.

entries.label: The travellers on the road
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA and Tabūk · described by pilgrims
entries.hint: Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Baṭṭūṭa passed through al-ʿUlA and Tabūk on the Hajj and left the classic descriptions of the corridor — Ibn Jubayr's account of the 'abode of Thamūd' at Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ among them.
entries.note: Ibn Jubayr, Riḥla; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, Riḥla.

entries.label: The epigraphy of the route
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The dated Kufic graffiti, read as historical documents, and the modern Saudi and international survey projects have made the northwestern routes one of the richest early-Islamic epigraphic landscapes anywhere in the world.
entries.note: the OCIANA and Saudi epigraphic projects; Imbert on the graffiti of the Hejaz routes.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The pilgrimage as the region's whole economy, the shrinking oasis farmland, and the subsidy that was the corridor's largest income

entries.label: The Hajj-service economy
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Provisioning the caravans, guiding and guarding them, keeping the wells, and selling dates and fodder to the pilgrims — the pilgrimage was the economy of the medieval northwest, and it arrived twice a year.
entries.note: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); F. E. Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

entries.label: The shrinking oasis farmland
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA, Taymāʾ, Khaybar and Wādī al-Qurā, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The date groves of the oases fed the towns and the caravans, but the irrigated area contracted over the medieval centuries as the population and the trade both fell — Wādī al-Qurā's 'villages' becoming fewer with each generation.
entries.note: the settlement archaeology of the oases; the medieval geographers on the decline of Wādī al-Qurā.

entries.label: The surra as the region's income
entries.loc: the northwestern routes
entries.hint: The annual subsidy from Damascus and Cairo to the tribes of the route was the largest single flow of money into the northwest — a corridor paid, year after year, to stay open.
entries.note: the surra literature; Petersen (2012).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The wells and reservoirs that made the crossing possible, and the oasis irrigation the communities maintained through every change of ruler

entries.label: The wells and reservoirs of the route
entries.loc: the Syrian and Egyptian Hajj roads
entries.hint: The deep wells, the plastered reservoirs (birak) and the catchment channels along the two pilgrim roads — the water technology, built and rebuilt by successive overlords, that made the twice-yearly crossing of the waterless corridor possible.
entries.note: Petersen (2012); the reservoir archaeology of the Syrian and Egyptian routes.

entries.label: The oasis irrigation, maintained
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA, Taymāʾ and Khaybar, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The underground channels and well-and-bucket systems of the oasis towns, kept working through political collapse and economic decline by the oasis communities themselves — the quiet engineering that kept the corridor's few settled places settled.
entries.note: the oasis hydrology surveys of al-ʿUlA and Khaybar.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The corridor between Syria, Egypt and the holy cities, the pilgrim as a carrier of goods and news, and the tribes' dealings with the two capitals

entries.label: The corridor between Syria, Egypt and the Ḥaramayn
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The region's whole medieval significance was as the ground the two great Hajj roads crossed — the link, twice a year, between the Mamluk metropolis at Cairo, the caravan city of Damascus, and the holy cities of the Hejaz.
entries.note: Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994); the route geography.

entries.label: The pilgrim as a carrier of goods and news
entries.loc: al-ʿUlA and Tabūk, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The caravans that crossed the northwest carried trade goods, letters, books and gossip between Cairo, Damascus and Mecca, and the towns of the route were where that traffic paused, resupplied and exchanged news.
entries.note: the studies of the Hajj as an information and trade network.

entries.label: The tribes and the two capitals
entries.loc: the northwestern routes · dealing with Damascus and Cairo
entries.hint: The tribes of the route dealt directly with Damascus and Cairo over the surra, the escort contracts and the compensation for a raided caravan — a small-power diplomacy conducted from the desert with the greatest states of the age.
entries.note: Faroqhi (1994); the Mamluk correspondence with the Hajj-road tribes.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A region defined entirely by what passed through it, the deep continuity of its tribal structure, and the handoff to the Ottoman Hajj machine

entries.label: A corridor, not a country
entries.loc: the northwestern corridor, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The medieval northwest had no state, no city of consequence and no history of its own beyond the two roads that crossed it — the clearest case in the peninsula of a region defined entirely by what passed through it.
entries.note: the historiographical point is made across the Hajj-road literature; the region has no medieval chronicle of its own.

entries.label: The deep continuity of the tribe
entries.loc: the northwestern steppe and oases
entries.hint: Through the caliphate, the Fatimids and the Mamluks, the human structure of the northwest — the tribes, the wells, the oasis families — barely changed. The overlords came and went; the corridor stayed the same.
entries.note: the ethnographic and tribal-history literature on the northern Hejaz.

entries.label: The thread continues — the Ottoman northwest and the railway
entries.loc: the northwestern corridor, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The folio ends in 1517, when the Ottomans took over the Hajj roads with Egypt. The Ottoman forts, the European travellers, the Hejaz Railway and the northwest's absorption into Saudi Arabia are covered in the Hejaz folios.
entries.note: a forward reference: hejaz-1517-1900 (which carries the northwest oases and Hajj-road material forward) is already built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The pilgrims on one of the hardest stretches of the road to Mecca, the tribes who guided and robbed them, and the oasis women and caravan slaves the sources pass over

entries.label: The pilgrims on the road
entries.loc: the northwestern Hajj routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The heat, the thirst, the bandits and the fever of Khaybar — the ordinary pilgrim's experience of the northwest was one of the hardest stretches of the journey to Mecca, and the chronicles and the graves along the route record how many did not make it.
entries.note: the Hajj-disaster and pilgrim-mortality notices in the chronicles; Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

entries.label: The tribes as guides and predators
entries.loc: the northwestern routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The men of the Balī, the Juhayna and the Banū ʿUqba who guided, watered and guarded the caravans for a fee — and raided them when the fee was short — living on both sides of the same transaction, generation after generation.
entries.note: Faroqhi (1994); the traveller accounts of the escort tribes.

entries.label: The oasis women and the caravan slaves
entries.loc: the oasis towns and the routes, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The women of the shrinking oasis towns, working the date harvest and the household, and the enslaved people moving with the caravans and the trade toward Egypt and the Hejaz — the people the geographers and the pilgrim narratives pass over almost entirely.
entries.note: the general household and slave-trade literature; the near-total silence of the sources on both.
